title: The one whose aim succeeds
hook: the naming; the brahmins read the marks: a great king or a great teacher

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven days. Maya died a week after the birth, and her sister raised him as her own. Your line was love can be adopted. Whose love did you notice? Day twenty-six.

Think about your own name. Someone chose it. Maybe after a grandparent, maybe from a book, maybe because it meant something, maybe because it just sounded good with your last name. Either way, somebody stood over you when you were tiny and decided what the world would call you. Every name carries a little wish in it. Today, the baby in the palace gets his. The king invites a hundred and eight brahmins to a feast, the story says, to name the child and to tell his future. Eight of them are the wisest. And they don't all agree.
screen: `SOMEONE CHOSE YOUR NAME.` → `A FEAST FOR THE NAMING.` → `EIGHT WISE MEN DISAGREE.`

segments.voice: The name they give him is Siddhattha, in Pali, or Siddhartha, in Sanskrit, the form most people know. Siddha means accomplished, succeeded. Attha means aim, goal, purpose. So Siddhattha is the one whose aim succeeds. The one who gets there. Gotama is the family name, and the Sakyas are his people, which is why he's later called Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas. Then the eight brahmins read his body. Buddhist texts describe thirty-two marks of a great man, signs a trained eye was said to recognize. The later tellings say seven of the brahmins raise two fingers: two possibilities. If he stays at home, he'll be a king who rules the whole world. If he leaves home, he'll be a buddha. The same prophecy his parents heard after the dream. But the youngest of the eight, a man named Kondañña, raises just one finger. He says there's only one road for this child. He will leave. He will become a buddha. Hold on to that name, Kondañña. He'll come back into the story much later, at a very important moment. Now picture the king hearing this. One road leads to an empire, his son on the throne, the family's future secure. The other leads out the palace gate, and away. You can guess which one a father would hope for. And that hope is going to shape everything the king does for the next twenty-nine years. For now, though, the baby just has a name. The one whose aim succeeds. A name that's also a wish, and, the story says, a promise.
screen: `SIDDHA + ATTHA: AIM SUCCEEDED.` · `THIRTY-TWO MARKS.` · `SEVEN RAISE TWO FINGERS.` · `KONDAÑÑA RAISES ONE.` · then, large: `A NAME IS A WISH.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you two minutes. Let the breath settle. Then say your own full name, slowly, out loud or silently. Every part of it. Listen to it as if you'd never heard it before. Who chose it? What might they have hoped for you? What wish is folded inside it? You don't have to agree with the wish. Just hear it. Then rest in the breath, and let your name go quiet. The bell holds the time.
Siddhattha. Siddhartha in Sanskrit: the one whose aim succeeds. The Buddha's given name, chosen at a feast where the wise men read his future.
Your line: a name is a wish. Today, use someone's name kindly and on purpose: a coworker, a cashier, a friend. Say it like it matters. Day twenty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhists know the Buddha as Siddhattha Gotama, or Siddhartha Gautama, and as Sakyamuni, the sage of the Sakyas; the naming and the reading of the marks are told in temple art and in stories for children.

fork.setup: you're Kondañña, the youngest brahmin. seven older, wiser men have raised two fingers: king or buddha. what do you do?
options: raise two fingers too. they're older.
raise one finger: he will become a buddha.
fork.reveal: he raises one finger. only one road for this child. and Kondañña will return, much later, at a very important moment.

trapdoor: what you thought: Siddhartha is just the Buddha's first name.
what it means: the one whose aim succeeds, a name that holds a wish, given at a feast where his future was read.

what a scholar hears: the name appears mainly in later biographies; the Nidanakatha tells of 108 brahmins, eight readers of the 32 lakkhaṇas, and Kondañña's single finger. the marks are listed in the Lakkhana Sutta (DN 30).

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka commentary): the naming and the eight brahmins
Lakkhana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 30): the thirty-two marks

notes: Naming feast with 108 brahmins, eight readers, Kondañña (the youngest) raising one finger: from the Nidanakatha as remembered. Confirm.
The name Siddhattha is rare in the early suttas and appears mainly in later texts; noted in the trapdoor. Confirm.
'Twenty-nine years' until the going forth is the traditional age (he left at 29). Confirm.
Kondañña's later role (first to understand the first sermon) is only foreshadowed.
